correctness.rationale: The core design is sound, but several P1 bugs in trigger logic (especially the 6-hour bound on cycle anchors and local date derivations for date-only tables) cause daytime events and journals to be misattributed or fall back to ET incorrectly.

robustness.rationale: Handles edge cases like DST artifacts and same-offset travel very well in the Python scripts. However, implicit timezone casting in timestamp subtraction and brittle noon-ET anchors reduce robustness.

scalability.rationale: Trigger-based approach is O(1) per write. Backfills use efficient window functions instead of O(N^2) trigger cascades. Python scripts paginate and maintain state efficiently.

idiomaticness.rationale: Excellent use of Postgres features like DISTINCT ON, window functions, and BEFORE triggers. Minor deductions for unsafe timestamp math.

response.summary: The implementation faithfully translates the ambitious ADR-0001 design into a working system. The tiered timezone resolution, the Python auto-population scripts, and the matrix view refactoring are exceptionally well executed. The `tz_log_gaps` view and the stateful `current_tz` tracking in the backfill scripts show a deep understanding of edge cases like DST artifacts and same-offset travel. However, there are a few load-bearing bugs in the SQL triggers. The most critical is a 6-hour bound in `cycle_offset_for_instant` that accidentally excludes almost all daytime events from the WHOOP cycle anchor, causing them to fall back to ET. Additionally, date-only tables (`journal_entries`, `habit_journal`, `whoop_journal`) struggle to project local dates correctly across the dateline due to brittle ET-clock assumptions. Fixing these trigger heuristics will bring the implementation to full correctness.

findings.title: WHOOP cycle anchor fails for daytime events due to strict 6h start_time bound
findings.description: The `dist_sec` calculation measures distance strictly to the cycle's `start_time` (bedtime). The `<= 6 * 60 * 60` filter means any event occurring more than 6 hours after bedtime (which includes almost all waking daytime hours) will fail to match the cycle, causing daytime events like meals and supplements to fall back to ET.
findings.recommendation: Remove the 6-hour filter and rely on `ORDER BY dist_sec ASC LIMIT 1` with a larger bound (e.g., 24 hours), or calculate distance to the closest of `start_time` or `end_time`.

findings.title: Unsafe TIMESTAMP minus TIMESTAMPTZ subtraction in garmin_activities
findings.description: The trigger subtracts `start_time_gmt` (TIMESTAMPTZ) from `start_time_local` (TIMESTAMP). This implicitly casts the TIMESTAMP to TIMESTAMPTZ using the server's `TimeZone` setting, which produces an incorrect interval if the server is not set to UTC.
findings.recommendation: Explicitly cast the GMT timestamp to UTC before subtracting: `NEW.start_time_local - (NEW.start_time_gmt AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')`.

findings.title: journal_entries backdating check compares local date to ET clock date
findings.description: The trigger tries to prevent overwriting dates on backdated entries by checking if `entry_date` matches the ET date of `notion_created_at`. Since `entry_date` is typed in local time, real-time entries made in distant timezones (e.g., Tokyo) will fail this check and incorrectly fall back to ET.
findings.recommendation: Call `derive_onyx_dates` first, then check if `NEW.entry_date` matches `d.onyx_behavioral_date` or `d.onyx_local_date` to determine if it was backdated.

findings.title: whoop_journal onyx_local_date is inconsistent for pre/post-midnight bedtimes
findings.description: The trigger derives dates using the cycle's `start_time` (bedtime). While `onyx_behavioral_date` correctly uses the -6h rule, `onyx_local_date` is set to the literal clock date of the bedtime. This splits a single behavioral day's journals across two local dates depending on whether bedtime was before or after midnight.
findings.evidence: NEW.onyx_local_date := d.onyx_local_date; (where d is derived from cycle_start_time)
findings.recommendation: For date-only behavioral tables, `onyx_local_date` should either mirror `onyx_behavioral_date` or be explicitly derived from the wake time, rather than the bedtime instant.

findings.title: habit_journal noon ET anchor shifts local dates in distant timezones
findings.description: When deriving `onyx_local_date` for a habit tap, the trigger anchors at noon ET of the `cycle_date` and converts to the local TZ. For timezones far from ET (like Tokyo +13h), noon ET falls into the next calendar day locally, shifting `onyx_local_date` forward by a day.
findings.evidence: noon_et := (NEW.cycle_date::timestamp + INTERVAL '12 hours') AT TIME ZONE 'America/New_York'; NEW.onyx_local_date := (noon_et AT TIME ZONE log_tz)::date;
findings.recommendation: Date-only sources cannot reliably project local dates across the dateline. Consider adding a `TIMESTAMPTZ` column to `habit_journal` to capture the exact tap instant.

things_done_well.title: Stateful current_tz tracking in Python backfills
things_done_well.why_it_matters: Seeding `current_tz` once and updating it in-memory prevents the script from missing return flights on the first run, and drastically reduces RPC round-trips to the database.

things_done_well.title: Clever DST artifact detection in tz_log_gaps
things_done_well.why_it_matters: By checking if the WHOOP offset matches the log offset at EITHER the start or end of the cycle, the view correctly identifies cycles that straddled a DST transition and hides them from the travel banner.

things_done_well.title: Synthesizing noon NY time for garmin_hrv fallback
things_done_well.why_it_matters: This elegant trick ensures `onyx_behavioral_date` matches the pre-attributed `calendar_date` across almost all timezones, while still allowing `user_tz_log` to resolve the correct provenance and ET date.

things_done_well.title: Elegant trips_view segmentation
things_done_well.why_it_matters: Using `generate_series` and window functions to group consecutive non-NY dates into trips is a highly idiomatic and efficient way to build a travel log from a continuous timezone series.

questions_for_followup: For date-only tables like `habit_journal` and `myfitnesspal_nutrition`, is there any plan to capture the actual `TIMESTAMPTZ` of the event in the future to avoid brittle noon-ET heuristics?

If a user travels to a timezone with an offset not present in `GENERIC_OFFSET_IANA` or their history, `whoop_tz_backfill.py` skips it. Is the expectation that the user will see the `/status` banner and manually add the entry, thereby teaching the script the new offset for future runs?
